events.description: 9/11 attacks; intended to push the US out of the region, out of the Arabian Peninsula, and end US support for Israel and Arab autocracies.
Zawahiri killed in Kabul, 21 years after 9/11; Roggio says this exposed that AQ's current leader is based in Iran and embarrassed the Taliban.
Right after the Taliban victory, Saif al-Adel issued an explicit call for supporters to migrate to Afghanistan to train to fight in Israel and elsewhere.
Nasir al-Wuhayshi, AQAP emir and AQ general manager, killed by the US (Roggio recalls '2016 or 17').

Latest UN 1267 Monitoring Team report: AQ central core assessed in decline, but AQIM passed a large portion of a $50M ransom up to AQ senior leadership; Houthis, AQAP and Shabaab cooperate on weapons smuggling; AQ training facilities in at least 13 of 34 Afghan provinces plus safe houses, madrasas, a weapons depot and facilitation routes into Iran.
actors: UN Security Council Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team

events.description: Al-Qaeda ejected the Islamic State after the disagreement between Baghdadi and al-Jolani (al-Sharaa).

Obama administration designated dozens of al-Qaeda operatives based in Iran and disclosed the 'secret deal' between al-Qaeda and Iran; Roggio checked a year ago and most are still alive as mid-to-high-level operatives.

About 1,500 Alawites killed in Syria ('last year'); Reuters traced responsibility to al-Sharaa's chain of command. Roggio: two massacres orchestrated by his people in the first eight months of his presidency.
Al-Sharaa invited to the White House; Trump gave him cologne; CENTCOM commander Admiral Cooper filmed shooting hoops with him.
Graeme Wood publishes 'What Happened to al-Qaeda' in The Atlantic, 25 years after 9/11.
Hamas attack on Israel, cited by Roggio as the cost of allowing a safe haven.

key_claims: Saif al-Adel is al-Qaeda's de facto but unannounced leader, based in Iran; the hosts debate whether the ambiguity is strategic (to protect the Taliban from pressure) or a sign of weakness, and Wood raises the possibility that his writings are even Iranian intelligence products.

Roggio rejects the 'core vs. branch' framing: al-Qaeda treats branches as theaters of operation, money flows up (AQIM ransom) and down, branch leaders (AQAP, AQIM, Shabaab) sit in the succession plan, and no branch except the ejected Islamic State has broken with AQ.

The UN Monitoring Team documents al-Qaeda training facilities in at least 13 of Afghanistan's 34 provinces, safe houses, madrasas, a weapons depot and facilitation routes into Iran, while the Taliban issues AQ members passports and IDs, pays them and uses AQ manuals in its forces.

Sirajuddin Haqqani is cited as an al-Qaeda member or strongly linked figure embedded in the Taliban government and security apparatus; anti-Taliban resistance groups (AFF, NRF, Sami Sadat's AUF) report fighting al-Qaeda fighters.

Wood: al-Qaeda failed its stated 25-year goal of forcing US political reversals via attacks, and new recruits now flow to affiliates or ISIS rather than AQ core ('old school podcasters who have lost their audience').

Roggio: AQ's goal (caliphate/sharia) never changed, only the path; Taliban rule in Afghanistan, Shabaab territory, JNIM's advance, Houthi cooperation and al-Sharaa in Damascus are what AQ success looks like.

Both hosts are skeptical of Ahmed al-Sharaa's transformation: his government includes SDGT-listed AQ-linked figures (including the TIP leader on AQ's shura), HTS units are in the security forces, and ~1,500 Alawites were killed under his chain of command.
Wood: al-Sharaa's rewards for renouncing AQ and ISIS's self-discrediting brutality have both worked against al-Qaeda's recruitment.
